curationMethod: Independent FAA official dated releases; paraphrases, not archived page bytes

claims.text: FAA's retrospectively updated timeline says it ordered temporary grounding of affected Boeing 737-9 MAX aircraft operated by US airlines or in US territory on January 6, 2024.
The January 6 FAA entry in its later-updated timeline says the emergency airworthiness directive required operators to inspect affected airplanes before further flight.
FAA announced it would audit the Boeing 737-9 MAX production line and suppliers to evaluate compliance with approved quality procedures.
FAA announced increased monitoring of in-service events and an assessment of independent oversight options for Boeing.
FAA said it required Boeing to provide additional data before approving an extensive inspection and maintenance process for returning 737-9 MAX aircraft to service.
FAA said it was requiring plug-door inspections of 40 aircraft after reviewing proposed inspection instructions.
FAA recommended visual inspection of door plugs on Boeing 737-900ER aircraft, noting that this is not part of the newer MAX fleet.
FAA said the 737-900ER shares the same door-plug design that motivated added safety recommendations after the January 5 incident.
FAA stated it would not grant Boeing any production expansion of the MAX, including the 737-9 MAX, while increasing oversight.
FAA approved inspection and maintenance procedures for grounded 737-9 MAX airplanes, which would be eligible to return to service after completion.

curatedEdges.basis: The January 12 release described withholding inspection-procedure approval pending more data; the January 24 release announced approval of a process.
January 12 introduced production and supplier oversight; January 24 added a no-expansion decision.
The January 21 recommendation addressed the distinct 737-900ER model sharing a door-plug design; this does not extend the 737-9 grounding order to that model.
